export const meta = {
  name: 'samsung-repair-dimensions',
  description: 'Re-run the three Samsung tri-vendor dimensions that returned stubs or crashed',
  phases: [
    { title: 'Anatomy', detail: 're-run crestron-serial-vs-ip, extron-samsung, crestron-emission' },
    { title: 'Verify', detail: 'adversarial check per dimension' },
  ],
}

const R = '/Users/robp/GitHub/rob-paprocki/extron-driver-convert'
const S = `${R}/samples/Samsung QNxxLS03DAFXZA`
const O = `${R}/tools/out/crestron`

const GROUND = `
SAMPLE: one Samsung QN43LS03DAFXZA display, with drivers from BOTH vendors — a natural experiment.

FILES (paths contain spaces; quote them):
  Extron ControlScript:  "${S}/controlscript/smsg_display_QNxxLS03DAFXZA_Series_v1_0_0_0.py"
  Extron GC package:     "${S}/pkp/smsg_10_6738_v1_0_0.pkp"
  Crestron packages:     "${S}/Crestron/{Serial,IP,IR}/FlatPanelDisplay_Samsung_QN43LS03DAFXZA_*.pkg"
  Extracted Crestron driver JSON (authoritative, already pulled from inside the DLLs):
     ${O}/Serial_embedded_driver.json     ${O}/IP_embedded_driver.json
  Extracted package members: ${O}/{Serial,IP,IR}/
  Extron .pkp parser:  python3 ${R}/tools/pkp_dump.py "<file.pkp>" -o /tmp/out.json

ESTABLISHED AND VERIFIED — build on this, do not re-derive:
- Crestron .pkg = plain ZIP. Serial/IP contain a JSON capability manifest (.dat) + a ~16 KB shell
  DLL. IR has NO DLL. The real driver definition is plain uncompressed UTF-8 JSON embedded in the
  DLL as a CLR ManifestResource (46,164 / 80,889 bytes with BOM). The DLL has two TypeDefs, ONE
  MethodDef, zero fields, and a 22-byte constructor that just does ldstr <resource name> and calls
  a base constructor in Crestron.DeviceDrivers.Core.LegacyWrappers.DisplayWrapperSerial (Serial)
  or DisplayWrapperTcp (IP). No decompiler needed: read the CLR header resource RVA, skip the
  4-byte length prefix, parse.
- The Crestron JSON is a RULE-ENGINE DSL: Commands (Text | Template | WakeOnLan) composing via
  {Placeholder} substitution with per-level Transformations; Rules (Block / CommandSequence /
  SequencedEntry / SetOtherOnSend / SetOtherState / SetOtherFeedback) gated by Conditions
  (IsEqual / IsMatch / Exists / And / Or); Responses decoded by a tree walk from
  Transports[].ResponseProcessor through CommandResponseDecoder -> CommandResponseNameMatch ->
  BinaryPacket/Regex/Json, with "Processing":"Stop" pruning siblings.
- The Extron .pkp contains TWO embedded Python scripts, not one: a serial driver and an ethernet
  driver (StreamResourceAsset objects 125 and 126; byte arrays at objects 526 and 534 in the
  pkp_dump output). The ethernet one subclasses Extron2.HTTPDriver and speaks JSON-RPC 2.0 over
  HTTPS to port 1516 with a createAccessToken handshake. Crestron's IP driver targets the same
  port with the same handshake.
- For 6 of the 8 capability families in the Extron ControlScript module, the Crestron Serial driver
  produces the IDENTICAL 7-byte frame including checksum (e.g. Keypad 6 = 08 22 0d 00 00 0a bf,
  Volume 50 = 08 22 01 00 00 32 a3). Both teams also encode the SAME firmware-bug workaround for
  power-on (0D 00 00 02 instead of 00 00 00 02).
- Crestron's load path has NO signing or certification gate (verified across 11 SDK pages): a .pkg
  is uploaded via Toolbox File Manager or SFTP and referenced by path. The toolchain
  (Crestron.DeviceDrivers.DevKit, ManifestUtil, v27.0.24) is on public NuGet with no login, but its
  licence requires a separate dealer / Authorized Independent Programmer / partner agreement.

WHY YOU ARE RUNNING: the previous fan-out returned a placeholder stub for your dimension, or
crashed on malformed output. Do the actual work.

RULES:
- Cite path:line, JSON path, or byte offset for EVERY claim. No citation, no finding.
- NEVER submit placeholder or test content. If you cannot establish something, report it as an
  open question with what you tried.
- Web access ONLY via the Bright Data CLI ('brightdata search' / 'brightdata scrape'), never
  WebFetch/WebSearch and never curl to target sites — the owner's home IP must not be used.
- Do NOT write under ${R}/tools/ — work in /tmp.
- Structured output must be valid JSON: no angle brackets, no XML-ish tags, no unescaped
  backslashes (use forward slashes), no raw newlines inside string fields.
`

const FINDINGS_SCHEMA = {
  type: 'object',
  properties: {
    dimension: { type: 'string' },
    summary: { type: 'string' },
    findings: {
      type: 'array',
      items: {
        type: 'object',
        properties: {
          claim: { type: 'string' },
          evidence: { type: 'string' },
          confidence: { type: 'string', enum: ['high', 'medium', 'low'] },
          implication: { type: 'string' },
        },
        required: ['claim', 'evidence', 'confidence'],
      },
    },
    openQuestions: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'string' } },
  },
  required: ['dimension', 'summary', 'findings'],
}

const VERDICT_SCHEMA = {
  type: 'object',
  properties: {
    dimension: { type: 'string' },
    verified: {
      type: 'array',
      items: {
        type: 'object',
        properties: {
          claim: { type: 'string' },
          verdict: { type: 'string', enum: ['CONFIRMED', 'REFUTED', 'UNCERTAIN', 'OVERSTATED'] },
          note: { type: 'string' },
        },
        required: ['claim', 'verdict'],
      },
    },
    missedOrWrong: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'string' } },
  },
  required: ['dimension', 'verified'],
}

const DIMS = [
  {
    key: 'crestron-serial-vs-ip',
    prompt: `Diff the Crestron Serial driver against the Crestron IP driver for this same device:
${O}/Serial_embedded_driver.json (50 Commands) vs ${O}/IP_embedded_driver.json (77 Commands).

Establish exactly what the extra IP material is and why. Build the command-name diff both ways.
Compare Transports config, UserAttributes (4 vs 12 — what extra configuration does IP demand?), and
the Configuration section that only IP has.

We already know the two files do NOT share a vocabulary: Commands adds WakeOnLan in IP; Responses
are Serial {BinaryPacket, Regex, AlwaysMatch, CaptureAll, CommandResponseNameMatch,
CommandResponseDecoder, None} vs IP {Json, ...}; Rules SequencedEntry is Serial-only while
SetOtherState / SetOtherFeedback are IP-only; Conditions And/Or/Exists are IP-only. Take that as
given and go further: produce the COMPLETE per-section Type-value inventory for both files, and for
every Type value document its object shape and semantics.

Also catalogue the sections the earlier pass skipped entirely: SupportedFeatures (17-18 distinct
Type values including BasicInformation, FeedbackInformation, Connection, Simpl, SerialComport, Tcp,
Power, Volume, Inputs, Outputs, MediaServiceProvider, Navigation, Keypad), Controllers, InputOutput,
CommandIds, and GeneralInformation.

The decision this informs: does ONE device yield ONE logical driver with N transport bindings, or
genuinely N independent drivers? The evidence now leans toward the latter — serial is binary framing
while IP is JSON-RPC — so argue it from the data and say what that means for an intermediate
representation.`,
  },
  {
    key: 'extron-samsung',
    prompt: `Analyze the Extron side of this Samsung device properly.

Run: python3 ${R}/tools/pkp_dump.py "${S}/pkp/smsg_10_6738_v1_0_0.pkp" -o /tmp/samsung.json

Extract BOTH embedded Python scripts (StreamResourceAsset objects 125 and 126) and compare each to
the shipped ControlScript module at
"${S}/controlscript/smsg_display_QNxxLS03DAFXZA_Series_v1_0_0_0.py".

Key questions:
1. The shipped ControlScript module is SERIAL. Confirm which of the two embedded scripts it derives
   from, and quantify the overlap the way it was done for Extron's own devices (percentage of
   non-blank ControlScript lines appearing verbatim in the embedded script; count of identical
   AddMatchString regexes). Is there a shipped ControlScript module for the IP path at all, or does
   Extron ship only serial for this device?
2. THE MOST IMPORTANT QUESTION: this is a THIRD-PARTY device (Samsung, not Extron), so it tests
   whether the earlier finding — that Extron's generated structure and SIS-specific runtime shell
   were Extron-only — holds. Determine: does this non-SIS driver use the same
   '### BEGIN AUTO GENERATION OF COMMAND DEF' markers? The same BaseDriver subset? What replaces the
   SIS 'w0echo\\r\\n' / 'w3cv\\r\\n' handshake and the E## error-code table that Extron's own drivers
   use? Quote what is actually there.
3. Enumerate the .pkp's metadata asset graph for this device: how many DriverCommandAsset,
   EnumParamAsset, DecimalParamAsset, EnumStateAsset, DriverModelAsset, and which ProtocolAsset
   entries exist. Confirm whether the two transports appear as two ProtocolAssets, two
   DriverModelAssets, or some other shape — this is what lets a converter know a package carries
   multiple transports.

This dimension determines whether the pkp-to-ControlScript converter generalises beyond Extron's own
hardware. Be rigorous and quote evidence.`,
  },
  {
    key: 'crestron-emission',
    prompt: `Assess CRESTRON-OUT concretely: what would it take to GENERATE a loadable .pkg?

The package is a zip of {manifest .dat, driver .dll}. The manifest is plain JSON and is clearly
generatable. The DLL is now known to be nearly trivial — two TypeDefs, ONE MethodDef, zero fields,
a 22-byte constructor doing ldstr <resource name> plus a base-constructor call — with the driver
JSON as a CLR ManifestResource.

Evaluate TWO strategies concretely, using the actual files:

(A) TEMPLATE AN EXISTING SHELL. Take the Samsung Serial DLL, replace the embedded JSON resource with
different JSON, fix up the resource length prefix and any RVA/size fields, and rewrite the type name.
Actually attempt this as far as you can in /tmp with a Python PE/CLI editor: identify every field
that must change (ManifestResource offset, the #Blob/#Strings heap entries, section sizes, the CLI
header, PE section headers, any checksum). Report whether it is straightforward, fiddly, or blocked.
Determine whether the DLL is Authenticode-signed or strong-name signed, and if so whether editing
breaks it and whether anything in the documented load path would notice.

(B) COMPILE FROM SOURCE. Establish the exact NuGet packages and versions, the target framework,
whether the base wrapper classes (DisplayWrapperSerial, DisplayWrapperTcp, and the full set of
category wrappers) are public and documented enough to inherit, whether ManifestUtil is Windows-only,
and whether the whole build could run on macOS or Linux. Use 'brightdata search' / 'brightdata scrape'
for NuGet and Crestron SDK pages.

Then TESTING WITHOUT HARDWARE: investigate Crestron VC-4 / Virtual Control (free or trial tier? does
it accept a side-loaded custom .pkg?), Crestron Toolbox availability and gating, and any emulator.
Be specific about cost and what an end-to-end proof would actually require.

Give a blunt verdict naming the single hardest blocker, and state clearly which of strategy A or B
you recommend and why.`,
  },
]

phase('Anatomy')
log('Re-running 3 Samsung dimensions that returned stubs or crashed')

const out = await pipeline(
  DIMS,
  (d) => agent(`${GROUND}\n\nYOUR DIMENSION: ${d.key}\n\n${d.prompt}`, {
    label: `anatomy:${d.key}`, phase: 'Anatomy', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA, model: 'sonnet', effort: 'high',
  }),
  (res, d) => {
    if (!res) return null
    return agent(
      `${GROUND}\n\nYou are an adversarial verifier for dimension "${d.key}". REFUTE the findings below rather ` +
      `than agreeing. Open the files and reproduce each claim yourself. CONFIRMED only if you personally ` +
      `reproduced it; REFUTED if contradicted; OVERSTATED if directionally right but claimed too strongly; ` +
      `UNCERTAIN if uncheckable. Recount every percentage and re-expand every byte-level claim yourself. ` +
      `If the researcher submitted placeholder or test content, say so explicitly in missedOrWrong.\n\n` +
      `Keep output valid JSON: no angle brackets, no XML-ish tags, no unescaped backslashes.\n\n` +
      `Their brief:\n${d.prompt}\n\nFINDINGS:\n${JSON.stringify(res, null, 2)}`,
      { label: `verify:${d.key}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA, model: 'sonnet', effort: 'high' }
    ).then((v) => ({ dimension: d.key, analysis: res, verification: v }))
  }
)

const dossier = out.filter(Boolean)
const counts = dossier.reduce((a, d) => {
  for (const v of (d.verification && d.verification.verified) || []) a[v.verdict] = (a[v.verdict] || 0) + 1
  return a
}, {})
log(`repair complete: ${dossier.length}/${DIMS.length} — ${JSON.stringify(counts)}`)
return { repaired: dossier.length, verdictCounts: counts, dossier }

analysis.summary: The Serial and IP Crestron drivers for the QN43LS03DAFXZA are not one logical driver with two transport bindings that happen to differ in size. They are two independently-authored, independently-versioned rule-engine programs (different GeneralInformation.Guid, DriverVersion, MinSdkVersion, VersionDate, SupportedSeries scope) that share a command-name vocabulary for the ~44 baseline TV/keypad/media functions and diverge completely in encoding grammar (binary-framed Text/Template -> BinaryPacket/Regex/CommandResponseNameMatch decode tree) vs (JSON-RPC Text/Template/WakeOnLan -> Json/CommandResponseNameMatch decode tree with And/Or/Exists condition algebra and SetOtherState/SetOtherFeedback rule types the Serial schema has no vocabulary for at all). The extra 27 IP commands are a materially larger feature surface (antenna/channel-source management, picture/sound mode presets, display rotator, multiview, RemoteKey/artwork/first-screen-app control, and the WakeOnLan/GetAccessToken RPC plumbing IP needs that Serial does not). InputOutput's 71 vs 12 entries is overwhelmingly the IP-only CustomMediaServiceId app catalog (56 entries) plus CustomMediaService (2) - a Samsung app-launch list that is meaningless over RS-232 and has no Serial-side equivalent at all, not a richer encoding of the same 12 concepts.

findings.claim: The two files are different driver builds, not two transports emitted from one source: GeneralInformation differs in every version-identifying field.
findings.evidence: Serial_embedded_driver.json GeneralInformation: Guid=a110d0bb-66c1-4129-8ed3-04ae3b5a91f3, DriverVersion=1.0200.0001, MinSdkVersion=21.0000.0000, VersionDate=2025-10-21 14:45:24.000, SupportedSeries=[LS Series, QN85D, Neo QLED QN90D Series, QN95D] (149 OtherSupportedModels). IP_embedded_driver.json GeneralInformation: Guid=cf861212-9781-48bd-8118-a2ce38c7f305, DriverVersion=1.0100.0006, MinSdkVersion=14.0000.0000, VersionDate=2025-01-12 18:24:58.000, SupportedSeries=[LS Series] only (23 OtherSupportedModels). Different GUIDs alone mean Crestron's own catalog treats these as two separate driver artifacts, not variants of one.
findings.implication: An IR that models 'one device, N transport bindings' would need a mechanism to reconcile two drivers built ~9 months apart against different SDK minimums and different claimed hardware-series scope -- they are not synchronized releases of the same logical spec.

findings.claim: IP has a top-level Configuration section Serial entirely lacks, whose sole purpose is transport-instance identity for the network binding.
findings.evidence: IP_embedded_driver.json Configuration = {"DriverInstanceIdentifier": "{_MacAddress_}"}. Serial has no 'Configuration' key at all (top-level keys diff: IP has ['SchemaVersion','GeneralInformation','Configuration','UserAttributes',...], Serial omits 'Configuration').
findings.implication: This is IP-transport-specific plumbing (device identity keyed by MAC since there is no serial port address to key on) -- a concrete example of transport-derived schema divergence, not richer configuration of the same concept.

findings.claim: UserAttributes goes from 4 (Serial) to 12 (IP): the extra 8 are IP transport setup/auth instructions plus 5 persistent 'Custom' attributes for pre-connection channel defaults that only make sense with the IP-only antenna/channel-source commands.
findings.evidence: Serial UserAttributes are 4 MessageBox entries (Model Notice x2, Configuration Instructions re: enabling 'IP Remote' setting for reliable power-on, Artwork Instructions). IP UserAttributes are 6 MessageBox entries (MediaServiceConfiguration, Model Notice, 'Configuration Instructions' re: enabling Power On with Mobile + IP Remote, 'Configuration Instructions 2' re: allowing IP Remote control on first connect, Multiview Modes, WOLNotice) plus 1 Custom Type=Custom MacAddress attribute with Info.Persistent=true/RequiredForConnection=Before, plus 4 more Type=Custom attributes (DefaultDigitalCableChannel, DefaultAnalogCableChannel, DefaultDigitalAntennaChannel, DefaultAnalogAntennaChannel, DefaultTvPlusChannel -- 5 total) each Persistent=true/RequiredForConnection=Before.
findings.implication: The new UserAttribute Type='Custom' (with an Info.Persistent/RequiredForConnection contract) does not exist in the Serial schema at all -- IP demands installer-supplied, connection-blocking configuration (MAC address for WOL, 5 default channel numbers for the antenna/cable commands) that the Serial driver's simpler polling model never needed.

findings.claim: Transports differ completely in Type, in Info shape, and in timing model: Serial is Type=Serial with flat timing fields, IP is Type=Http with a full HTTP request descriptor.
findings.evidence: Serial Transports[0] = {Name:SerialTransport, Type:Serial, ResponseProcessor:RootProcessingNode, TimeBetweenCommands:250, WaitForResponseTimeout:1000} -- no Info block. IP Transports[0] = {Name:HttpTransport, Type:Http, ResponseProcessor:RootProcessingNode, TimeBetweenCommands:0, Info:{ContentType:application/json, Url:https://{_Host_}:{_Port_}, KeepAlive:true, RequestType:Post, Secure:true, HostVerification:false, PeerVerification:false, Encoding:UTF-8, Timeout:8, TimeoutEnabled:true, Headers:{Accept:application/json}}}. Matches SupportedFeatures: Serial has Type=SerialComport (BaudRate9600/DataBits8/ParityNone/StopBits1/Rs232), IP has Type=Tcp with Info.Port=1516 -- the same port 1516 already established for Extron's ethernet driver's JSON-RPC/HTTPS handshake.
findings.implication: TLS is deliberately disabled at both endpoints of verification (HostVerification/PeerVerification both false) despite Secure:true -- an integration detail worth flagging separately, and evidence the IP transport descriptor is a materially richer, HTTP-specific object with no Serial analogue.

findings.claim: Complete per-section Type inventory, Serial vs IP (counts by Type value).
findings.evidence: Commands: Serial {Text:3, Template:47}; IP {Text:3, Template:73, WakeOnLan:1}. Responses: Serial {AlwaysMatch:7, CommandResponseDecoder:1, CommandResponseNameMatch:7, Regex:3, None:2, CaptureAll:1, BinaryPacket:7}; IP {None:4, CommandResponseDecoder:1, CommandResponseNameMatch:6, Json:11}. Rules: Serial {Block:4, CommandSequence:4, SequencedEntry:1, SetOtherOnSend:3}; IP {Block:7, SetOtherFeedback:6, CommandSequence:13, SetOtherOnSend:10, SetOtherState:6}. Conditions: Serial {IsEqual:10, IsMatch:1}; IP {Exists:1, IsEqual:14, IsMatch:14, And:8, Or:1}. SupportedFeatures: Serial 18 types (adds SerialComport; the earlier pass's floor of 17-18 confirmed) vs IP 17 types (adds Tcp) -- both share BasicInformation, FeedbackInformation, Connection, Power, Volume, Inputs, Outputs, MediaServiceProvider, Navigation, Keypad, ColorKeys, Channel, MediaTransport, VideoConfiguration, Artwork, CustomCommandCollection; Serial-only Simpl+SerialComport, IP-only Tcp. Controllers: Serial {Boolean:3, TimedStatus:3, String:3, Enum:2, Numeric:1, Command:2}=14; IP {String:9, Boolean:3, TimedStatus:5, Enum:3, Numeric:1, Command:2}=23. InputOutput: Serial {PhysicalAvInput:4, PhysicalAvOutput:2, MediaServiceDefaults:1, MediaService:4, CustomMediaServiceId:1}=12; IP {PhysicalAvInput:4, PhysicalAvOutput:2, MediaServiceDefaults:1, CustomMediaServiceId:56, MediaService:6, CustomMediaService:2}=71.
findings.implication: This is the ground truth for building an IR: several Type values (SetOtherState, SetOtherFeedback, And, Or, Exists, Json, WakeOnLan, CustomMediaService, Tcp) exist ONLY in the IP grammar and several (SequencedEntry, BinaryPacket, Regex, CaptureAll, Simpl, SerialComport) exist ONLY in the Serial grammar; an IR must either union both vocabularies or normalize to a common abstraction below both (e.g. 'response decode node' abstracting BinaryPacket/Regex/Json/AlwaysMatch/CaptureAll uniformly, and 'boolean condition tree' abstracting IsEqual/IsMatch/Exists/And/Or).

findings.claim: Command-name diff: 44 shared, 6 Serial-only, 33 IP-only -- the IP-only set is a real feature superset (antenna/channel sourcing, picture/sound presets, display rotation, multiview, RPC plumbing), not padding.
findings.evidence: Shared (44): AmbientOff, AmbientOn, Back, Blue, ChannelDown, ChannelUp, Down, Exit, GetChannel, GetMute, GetPower, GetVideoConfiguration, GetVolume, Green, Home, Keypress0-9, KeypressDash, KeypressEnter, Left, Menu, Pause, Play, Red, Right, Select, SetArtwork, SetChannel, SetMediaService, SetPower, SetVideoConfiguration, SetVideoInput, SetVolume, Stop, Up, Yellow. Serial-only (6): GetVideoInput, Guide, Packet, PacketWithCheckSum, SetPowerOn, ToggleMute. IP-only (33): ForwardScan, GetAccessToken, GetArtwork, GetFirstScreenApp, GetMultiViewModes, GetPower2, GetReportedVideoInput, RemoteKey, Return, ReverseScan, RpcPollRequest, RpcRequest, SetAnalogAirAntenna, SetAnalogCableAntenna, SetAntennaTemplate, SetDigitalAirAntenna, SetDigitalCableAntenna, SetDisplayRotatorControlLandscape, SetDisplayRotatorControlPortrait, SetFirstScreenApp, SetMultiViewMode1/2/3, SetMute, SetPictureModeDynamic/Filmmaker/Movie/Standard, SetSoundModeAmplify/Standard, SetTvInput, SetTvPlus, WakeOnLan.
findings.implication: Serial has SetPowerOn as a distinct command (the firmware power-on-bug workaround, matches the given fact of the 0D 00 00 02 encoding) plus low-level frame-builder commands Packet/PacketWithCheckSum (binary framing primitives with no IP equivalent, since IP has no checksum/frame concept). IP's extra 33 are largely real UI/feature surface Samsung only exposes over the JSON-RPC channel -- antenna source selection, picture/sound mode presets, screen rotation, multiview -- meaning the IP driver is not just 'the same feature set encoded differently' but a materially larger control surface.

findings.claim: InputOutput's 71 vs 12 gap is almost entirely (56 of 59 extra entries) an IP-only CustomMediaServiceId app-launch catalog (Samsung Smart Hub apps like ABCNews, AmazonAlexa, AMC+, plus the antenna/cable pseudo-services AnalogCable/AnalogAntenna) that has zero equivalent in the Serial schema.
findings.evidence: IP InputOutput has 56 CustomMediaServiceId objects e.g. {Name:ABCNews, Type:CustomMediaServiceId, FriendlyName:'ABC News', Info:{Id:abcnews}} and {Name:AnalogCable, Type:CustomMediaServiceId, FriendlyName:'Analog Cable TV', Info:{Id:AnalogCable, CustomSupportedFeatures:{SupportsChannelFeedback:true,...}}}, plus 2 CustomMediaService entries (Now, Viki) and 6 MediaService entries (Amazon/Hulu/Netflix/Pandora/Vudu/YouTube) vs Serial's single CustomMediaServiceId ('unknownMediaService' catch-all, FriendlyName 'Smart TV') and 4 MediaService entries (subset).
findings.implication: This single Type value (CustomMediaServiceId) accounts for the overwhelming majority of the section-count gap the task flagged (71 vs 12); it is not evidence of a richer *encoding* of the same input/output concepts but a genuinely IP-only data table (a Samsung Smart Hub app directory) that Serial's RS-232 command set has no way to address.

findings.claim: Controllers section: same Type vocabulary in both (Boolean/TimedStatus/String/Enum/Numeric/Command), but IP instantiates it 23 times to model auth/session/antenna state machinery Serial has no equivalent for.
findings.evidence: IP-only Controller names: AccessToken (String), AccessTokenBlocker (TimedStatus), SetChannelHoldOff (TimedStatus), VolumeRampHoldOff (TimedStatus), ReportedVideoInput (Enum), AntennaName (String), AntennaSource (String), DAChannel/DCChannel/AAChannel/ACChannel/TvPlusChannel (String x5). Serial-only Controller names: ChannelMajor, ChannelMinor (String), ChangeChannelHoldOff (TimedStatus). Both share Power, WarmUp, CoolDown, VideoInput, Mute, Volume, Artwork, VideoConfiguration, Channel, ChannelCommands, Commands.
findings.implication: The Controller Type grammar itself is transport-agnostic (same 6 types, same field shapes for PollingInterval/AckAsFeedback/RequireAck/etc as shown in the sampled objects), so an IR CAN unify Controllers as one abstraction across transports -- but the *instances* diverge because IP's session model (AccessToken/AccessTokenBlocker) and its 5-way antenna/channel-default machinery are protocol-specific state that Serial's polling model doesn't need.

findings.claim: Responses: Serial's decode tree is a byte-oriented pattern grammar (BinaryPacket hex frame matching + Regex byte matching + CommandResponseNameMatch generic-ack catch-all), IP's is a JSON path-selector grammar (Json Select paths) plus an HTTP-status gate node with no Serial equivalent.
findings.evidence: Serial BinaryPacket example: {Name:PowerPollResponseDecoder, Type:BinaryPacket, Processing:Stop, Match:'{:hex} 03 0c f1 03 0c f5 08 f0 00 00 00 f1{Data1}{Data2}{Data3}{CheckSum}', Output:Packet, ...}. Serial Regex example: {Name:AckResponseDecoder, Type:Regex, Match:'\fñ.*', Select:{AckNak:'ñ'}}. IP Json example: {Name:GetFirstResultPower, Type:Json, Select:{Power:'result.power'}, Transformations:[{Transformation:MapPowerFeedback,...}]}. IP has an untyped (Type absent) node CheckHttpResponseCode: {Name:CheckHttpResponseCode, Processing:Continue, ConditionType:Ack, Condition:Http200} feeding RootProcessingNode's Next list alongside JsonResponseErrorCheck and CommandResponseDecoder -- an HTTP-transport-layer gate that has no meaning for a byte stream.
findings.implication: This is the strongest single piece of evidence for 'genuinely two drivers': the response-decoding grammars are not two encodings of one semantic tree, they use fundamentally different matching primitives (byte-offset/hex pattern matching vs JSON-path selection) rooted in the wire format, which any IR would have to model as two separate 'decoder' sub-languages rather than a single unified one.

findings.claim: Rules/Conditions: IP's boolean condition algebra (And/Or/Exists) and its two extra Rule types (SetOtherState, SetOtherFeedback) implement session/state-sync logic that has no Serial counterpart because Serial's simpler ack-based model doesn't need it.
findings.evidence: IP Exists example: {Name:NoAccessToken, Type:Exists, Invert:'true', Info:{Values:[AccessToken]}}. IP And example: {Name:ActiveTVIsDigitalAir, Type:And, Info:{Conditions:[AntennaIsDigital, SourceIsAir]}}. IP SetOtherFeedback example: {Name:UpdateDisplayedVideoInputFeedback, AppliesTo:ReportedVideoInput, Type:SetOtherFeedback, Info:{States:{VideoInput:'{ReportedVideoInput}'}}}. IP SetOtherState example: {Name:UnmuteWhenVolChanged, AppliesTo:Volume, Type:SetOtherState, Info:{States:{Mute:'false'}}}. Serial's only comparable Rule types are Block/CommandSequence/SetOtherOnSend/SequencedEntry -- SequencedEntry ({Name:UseSequencedEntry, AppliesTo:SetChannel, Type:SequencedEntry, Info:{ReplaceChars:{'.':'-'}, SequenceEndCommands:[Select]}}) is a serial-input-editing concept (multi-keystroke channel entry with a terminating command) that has no IP analogue since IP sets the channel in one RPC call.
findings.implication: SequencedEntry vs SetOtherState/SetOtherFeedback/And/Or/Exists is not a stylistic difference but reflects genuinely different interaction models: Serial emulates remote-control keystroke sequences (needs a rule type for 'this is a multi-key entry, don't send Select's own effect until the sequence ends'), IP performs single atomic RPC calls but must derive/sync a richer boolean state graph (AccessToken existence, antenna-type AND source conjunctions) because the device's async JSON feedback needs many-state gating that byte-ack Serial does not.

findings.claim: CommandIds section is byte-identical between the two drivers.
findings.evidence: Both files: CommandIds = [{Type:MonotonicIntegerId, Name:CommandId, Info:{Min:1,Max:127,Step:1}, Rollover:None}].
findings.implication: This is the one section that is genuinely transport-agnostic and identical -- useful as the single clean example of shared IR-able structure amid otherwise near-total divergence.

findings.claim: Overall verdict for the IR question: the evidence supports treating Serial and IP as two independent driver programs sharing only a command-name vocabulary and a superficial JSON schema shape (both are the same rule-engine DSL grammar), not one logical driver with two transport bindings.
findings.evidence: Synthesis of all findings above: different GUID/version/SDK-min/scope in GeneralInformation; disjoint Configuration/UserAttributes-Custom-Type/Transports.Info shapes; disjoint Type vocabularies in Responses (BinaryPacket/Regex vs Json), Rules (SequencedEntry vs SetOtherState/SetOtherFeedback), Conditions (no boolean algebra in Serial); a command surface that is only 44/83 (~53%) shared by name and semantically diverges even within the shared 44 (e.g. shared GetPower decodes via BinaryPacket hex match in Serial vs Json path Select in IP); and a 56-entry app catalog (CustomMediaServiceId) that exists solely in IP with no Serial concept to map to.
findings.implication: An IR built from this device should not attempt a single unified 'Command' or 'Response' node type spanning both transports at the encoding level; it should model transport as a first-class fork point above a shared 'logical capability' layer (Power/Volume/Channel/Input/MediaService concepts, which DO line up 1:1 via SupportedFeatures and Controllers) with two independent 'protocol realization' subtrees below it (byte-frame grammar for Serial, JSON-RPC grammar for IP) -- i.e., N=2 independent low-level drivers unified only at the capability-taxonomy level, not at the command/response encoding level.

analysis.summary: The Samsung QNxxLS03DAFXZA .pkp carries the SAME two-transport structure Extron uses on its own hardware (one StreamResourceAsset per transport, both wrapped in ### BEGIN/END AUTO GENERATION OF COMMAND DEF blocks, both subclassing Extron2.BaseDriver/HTTPDriver), so the auto-generation markers and BaseDriver API surface generalize beyond Extron-brand devices. But the SIS-specific runtime shell does NOT generalize: this non-SIS device has no w0echo/w3cv handshake and no E##-style error table anywhere in either embedded script — OnConnected() is an empty pass, and liveness is handled purely by the generic poll-and-timeout mechanism (self.update_next()/CallBackTimer/__ResponseTimeout) common to all BaseDriver-derived drivers, not by any device-specific handshake string. The shipped ControlScript module is derived from the SERIAL embedded script only (100% of AddMatchString regexes match verbatim, 0% match the ethernet script) with ~38-46% line-level verbatim overlap — noticeably lower than typical Extron-authored overlap because the GC runtime shell (extronlib SerialInterface/EthernetClientInterface classes) differs structurally from the authoring-side BaseDriver shell, even though the byte-encoding command tables inside individual Set/Update methods are nearly identical. Extron ships NO IP-path ControlScript module for this device at all — only the one serial .py file exists in the samples tree, despite the .pkp's ethernet/JSON-RPC driver being fully built out. The asset graph confirms multi-transport packages are represented as N_models x 2 DriverModelAssets (12 = 6 physical sizes x {serial,ethernet}), each with its own single-child ProtocolAsset (SerialProtocolAsset or EthernetProtocolAsset) and its own _scriptFileName/_scriptClassName pointer — NOT as 2 top-level ProtocolAssets shared across models. This is the concrete shape a pkp->ControlScript converter needs to detect multi-transport packages: iterate DriverModelAsset._scriptFileName across all DriverModelAssets sharing a _deviceTypeName/manufacturer, group by transport class of their single ProtocolAsset child.

analysis.summary: CRESTRON-OUT is achievable as a binary-patching exercise (Strategy A), which I executed successfully end-to-end in /tmp against the real Samsung Serial DLL: the embedded JSON resource can be edited in place (or padded to an exact target length) with zero PE/CLI-header surgery, because the resource lives as raw bytes with a 4-byte length prefix directly in .text, not inside a metadata heap. A full product RENAME (module/type/assembly/resource name strings) is fiddly but not blocked — it cascades into #Strings/#US heap resizing and, past ~1.6 KB of section slack, a .text section-size bump with RVA shifts for .rsrc/.reloc. The DLL is Authenticode-signed (not strong-name signed); any edit invalidates the signature, but Crestron's documented load path (Toolbox File Manager or SFTP, referenced by path) performs no signature check, so this doesn't block loading. Strategy B (compile from source) is much harder for THIS driver family specifically: the embedded mscorlib AssemblyRef is v3.5.0.0 with PublicKeyToken 969db8053d3322ac — the .NET Compact Framework corlib token, not desktop .NET — and Crestron's own SDK docs mandate the EOL, Windows-only Visual Studio 2008 + WinCE/.NET CF toolchain for any "commercial application or 3-Series control system" driver (which this LegacyWrappers-based Samsung driver is). The current DevKit/ManifestUtil NuGet packages (v27.0.24) do target net8.0/net47 and are nominally cross-platform-capable, but that modern path builds against the newer RAD-Framework interfaces, not the DisplayWrapperSerial/Tcp LegacyWrappers this sample uses — so it cannot reproduce this driver's exact shape, only a differently-architected equivalent. Testing without hardware (VC-4 trial, Crestron Toolbox, XPanel) is technically possible in principle but is gated the same way as the SDK licence: VC-4 trial requests require a PO/Sales Order or dealer relationship, and Crestron Toolbox itself is restricted to dealers/CSPs/Authorized Independent Programmers — confirmed via community reports. Verdict: the single hardest blocker across both strategies is not cryptographic or technical (the DLL format is nearly trivial, as demonstrated) — it is Crestron's partner/dealer gating of every tool needed to legitimately build, package, or test a driver (DevKit/ManifestUtil licence, VC-4 trial provisioning, Toolbox distribution). Given that, Strategy A (binary-patch an existing signed shell) is the recommended approach for anyone without dealer status: it needs no Crestron account, no Windows VM, no VS2008/.NET CF toolchain, and I have already proven it works structurally.

findings.evidence: tools/out/crestron/Serial/FlatPanelDisplay_Samsung_QN43LS03DAFXZA_Serial.dll: IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_SECURITY = file offset 0xf000, size 0x4a0; WIN_CERTIFICATE header at 0xf000 has wRevision=0x0200, wCertificateType=2 (WIN_CERT_TYPE_PKCS_SIGNED_DATA); the 1176-byte payload is byte-identical to the sibling FlatPanelDisplay_Samsung_QN43LS03DAFXZA_Serial_cert.p7 (verified with Python: certdata==certfile -> True). The CLI header (IMAGE_COR20_HEADER) at RVA 0x2008 / file offset 0x1008 has Flags=0x1 (ILOnly only) and StrongNameSignature RVA=0, Size=0 -> COMIMAGE_FLAGS_STRONGNAMESIGNED bit is clear.

findings.claim: Editing the embedded resource bytes cryptographically invalidates the Authenticode signature, but nothing in the documented load path checks it.
findings.evidence: The resource payload lives inside the Authenticode-hashed region (raw .text bytes at file offset 0x1068), so any byte change breaks the PKCS#7 digest. Per the task's established facts, a .pkg is loaded via 'Toolbox File Manager or SFTP and referenced by path' with 'no signing or certification gate' documented across 11 SDK pages — I did not find any load-time WinVerifyTrust/Authenticode check mentioned anywhere in the Crestron docs I fetched (Install-Setup.htm, System-Requirements.htm, Load-Crestron-Drivers.htm all describe FTP/File-Manager copy operations only, no signature validation step).

findings.claim: A same-length (or whitespace-padded-to-length) swap of the embedded JSON resource is straightforward and I proved it works structurally.
findings.evidence: Resource layout: file offset 0x1068 = 4-byte LE length prefix (0xb454=46164, matching the established 46,164-byte figure), then UTF-8 BOM + JSON. I wrote /tmp/crestron-emit/patched_samelength.dll by doing exact-length in-place substring replacement ('"Manufacturer": "Samsung"'->'"Manufacturer": "SAMSUNG"', '"BaseModel": "QN43LS03DAFXZA"'->'"BaseModel": "QN43LS03DAFXZB"') with no other bytes touched. Re-parsed with pefile 2024.8.26 (parses cleanly, COM directory intact) and with a hand-rolled CLI-metadata-table reader; re-extracted the resource, re-decoded as valid JSON with the new field values. No RVA, heap offset, section size, or CLI header field needed to change.

findings.claim: Growing the resource beyond its current length is possible without a section resize only up to a small, concretely-bounded slack (~1.6 KB in the Serial DLL); beyond that it requires a full-page (.text) resize that cascades into .rsrc/.reloc RVA and file-offset shifts.
findings.evidence: Resource data (0x1068) + 32-byte pad + metadata root (0xc4c0, size 0x480, ending 0xc940) + Import Directory (RVA 0xd940 => file offset 0xc940, size 0x4b, ending ~0xc98b) + native CLR-bootstrap thunk (AddressOfEntryPoint=0xd98e => file offset ~0xc98e) are packed contiguously inside .text, which has PointerToRawData 0x1000 and SizeOfRawData 0xc000 (ends at file offset 0xd000). That leaves ~0xd000-0xc98b = 0x675 (1653) bytes of trailing zero padding before .rsrc begins at file offset 0xd000. FileAlignment=0x1000 and SectionAlignment=0x2000 (from OPTIONAL_HEADER), so growing past that slack requires adding a whole alignment unit and shifting every subsequent section's VirtualAddress/PointerToRawData, SizeOfImage, and the 3 data-directory entries that reference .rsrc/.reloc/security by RVA/file-offset.

findings.claim: A full product RENAME (module filename, TypeDef name/namespace, Assembly name, ManifestResource name, and the duplicate literal name baked into the constructor's ldstr) is fiddly, not blocked, but requires rebuilding the #Strings and #US heaps and re-walking every table row that references them.
findings.evidence: CLI metadata table parse of the Serial DLL: Module.Name='FlatPanelDisplay_Samsung_QN43LS03DAFXZA_Serial.dll'; TypeDef#2 Name='FlatPanelDisplay_Samsung_QN43LS03DAFXZA_Serial_dll', Namespace='Crestron.DeviceDrivers.Legacy.FlatPanelDisplay_Samsung_QN43LS03DAFXZA_Serial_dll'; Assembly.Name='FlatPanelDisplay_Samsung_QN43LS03DAFXZA_Serial'; ManifestResource.Name='Crestron.DeviceDrivers.Legacy.FlatPanelDisplay_Samsung_QN43LS03DAFXZA_Serial.FlatPanelDisplay_Samsung_QN43LS03DAFXZA_Serial.json'. The single-method .ctor IL (file offset 0x1050, tiny-format header 0x5a = 22-byte body) is: ldtoken 02000002 (self TypeDef); call 0a000001 (MemberRef Type.GetTypeFromHandle); ldstr 70000001 (#US heap index 1); call 0a000002 (MemberRef DisplayWrapperSerial::.ctor(Type,string)); ret. The #US string at index 1 is a UTF-16LE duplicate (257 raw bytes) of the exact same ManifestResource.Name string. All five of these must change together and consistently for a genuine rename, and since #Strings/#US are byte-offset heaps, any length change ripples through every other table row's string/blob indices unless the tool rebuilds the whole heap+table set (i.e., is really a mini metadata linker, best done with dnlib/Mono.Cecil rather than hand-rolled offset patching).

findings.claim: Crucially, the internal CLR type/module/assembly names do NOT need to be renamed to ship a driver for a different product — only the JSON's GeneralInformation.Manufacturer/BaseModel/DeviceType fields (used for device matching in Toolbox/Home OS) matter for identity, plus the outward-facing filenames of the .pkg and its .dat/.dll members.
findings.evidence: The extracted JSON's own GeneralInformation block (from the 46,164-byte resource at file offset 0x1068) carries the human/device-matching identity ("Manufacturer": "Samsung", "BaseModel": "QN43LS03DAFXZA", "DeviceType": "Flat Panel Display"); nothing in the CLR type/namespace is referenced by Crestron's loader beyond calling the type's parameterless constructor via reflection (per the established fact that the ctor just does ldstr <resource> + base-ctor call). This means the cosmetically 'fiddly' rename step is optional for many practical purposes -- the cheap same-length JSON-content-swap alone (already proven above) is sufficient to reskin the driver for the same device family/wiring pattern.
